what: Topology-optimisation validation model: the tall tripod (spec 5.3).
why: Raising the camera to 201 mm puts a real three-dimensional load path between the mount and the floor, and how to build it -- one column, three legs, a braced tripod, something else -- is genuinely open.
caveat: This is a validation model, not the shipped bracket. osmo_tripod/osmo_tripod.scad stays as it is.
units: mm / N / MPa (lengths mm, forces N, stresses MPa)

material.name: PLA
material.notes: Stiffest common filament, but creeps under sustained load and softens in a hot car / direct sun. Fine for jigs and dry indoor parts; wrong for anything structural left loaded for days.

conditions.model: equivalent solid, high density, generous perimeters

printer.name: Bambu Lab X1-Carbon
printer.note: AMS-fed; the purge tower needs ~60x60 mm of plate on multi-material prints.

manufacturing.build_axis_note: Printed standing up, the way the model is drawn: the layer planes are horizontal, so bending the structure pulls the layers apart. That is the worst orientation for an FFF part and is exactly what this model is meant to expose. `build_axis` is also which way is *down* for ground contact.

requirements.safety_factor_note: materials.required_safety_factor() asks for 4.0 while the PLA card is provisional (no value measured on this printer). 3.0 is kept here so the number stays comparable with the recorded runs; the report states the shortfall.
requirements.deflection_note: At 201 mm the camera is a long lever. 3 mm at the camera top is about 0.9 degrees of tilt, which is where video framing visibly drifts.

cases.name: LC1f  push 1.0 N horizontally at the camera mount
cases.represents: 1.0 N is the tipping limit, and the tipping limit is what bounds the load on this model -- it is not a strength case, because past it the part is lying on the floor. tall_tripod.scad computes the BEST-CASE tipping force (feet on the rim of the design space): 1.025 N. The actual value depends on where the optimiser puts the feet and is only known after the run -- read `ground_contact` in the summary.
cases.load_note: 1.0 N forward at the head plus the 0.35 kg camera weight (3.44 N down). The horizontal force is applied at the head because that is where preserve is; the moment it stands in for is 1.0 N x 65 mm of remaining lever to the camera top.

cases.name: LC2   camera weight plus 5x vertical shock
cases.represents: Setting the tripod down hard, or a knock straight down. 5 g is the usual screening factor for a hand-carried item.

cases.name: LC3n  lift by the head, north foot caught
cases.represents: Picking the tripod up by the camera while one leg is still hooked on something. This is the case that decided the mass of the short tripod, and the only kind of case here that asks for a wide base -- everything else is happiest with a single central post. Three of them, one per catch zone, because the hooked leg can be any of them and one case alone just moves the post over to that zone (measured -- see the catch-zone note in `regions`).

cases.name: LC3sw lift by the head, south-west foot caught
cases.load_note: The 4 N horizontal component points away from the caught foot, as in LC3n, rotated with the zone.

cases.name: LC3se lift by the head, south-east foot caught
LC4t  twist the head about the vertical axis
cases.represents: Tightening the thumb screw, or panning the camera against friction. A hollow section is stiff in bending and can still be soft in torsion, so this case is what stops the optimiser producing an open C-section.
cases.load_note: A 3 N couple across the head: +Y on the +X half, -Y on the -X half, about 10 mm apart. Combined with the camera weight so the case is a real one rather than pure torsion.

design_settings.symmetry_note: No mirror symmetry declared. The three LC3 cases each load one side and LC4t twists; mirror-averaging would pull the result away from what those cases actually ask for. It would also decide part of the stance, which is the thing v4 exists to stop doing.
design_settings.voxel_note: A COARSE EXPLORATORY GRID, chosen deliberately. 10 mm across a d240 x 146 design space is 24 cells wide and about 6,600 cells in the domain -- enough to see which topology the loads ask for, and not enough to size a member. Override it from the command line with `--voxel`; `topopt setup` times one solve on whatever grid it builds and prints what 80 iterations would cost, so the trade is priced before it is paid rather than after.

design_freedom.note_ground_zones: 4 support(s) act on the build plane rather than on preserve, so where the part touches down is a result. The zones themselves are still an input: this study says to look for contact inside them.
design_freedom.note_fixed_points: 3 load/support footprint(s) sit on preserve at positions the CAD model chose. The optimiser decides how to reach them, not where they are.

printer.name: Bambu Lab X1-Carbon
printer.note: AMS-fed; the purge tower needs ~60x60 mm of plate on multi-material prints.

build_volume.voxel_vs_min_feature: one voxel is 10.00 mm and the smallest printable wall is 0.80 mm, so the grid cannot represent the printer's limit; minimum-feature checks on this run are about the grid, not the machine.

setup_warnings: the free region is only 2.0 voxels (20.00 mm) thick at its thinnest. Below about 3 voxels there is no room for a hole, so the topology there is set by the outline rather than chosen -- refine the grid or widen the design space.

4 support(s) use ground contact, so the feet are not placed by the CAD. What the study still chooses is the 4 zone(s) to look in (ground_all at [0.0, 0.0, 5.0]; catch_n at [0.0, 80.7, 5.0]; catch_sw at [-69.6, -38.0, 5.0]; catch_se at [69.6, -38.0, 5.0]). If a partial-support case appears at only one azimuth, check the result actually stands up -- a glued contact cannot tip, so nothing in the objective asks for a wide stance.
